EDS AI Workflow (Eitri Agentic Dev Workflow)

Add your team’s context

The harness needs relevant business domain information, standards, policies and conventions before decisions depend on them. Context supports correct behaviour, but does not guarantee it. This page shows where each kind of context enters the PO/BA and developer harnesses, and how a team adds its own.

For how to organise instructions so an agent loads only what it needs, read Give agents the right context. Exact file names, registry entries and environment settings are in the harness repository.

AIHow AI can help in this chapter

  • Apply domain knowledge
  • Use relevant standards
  • Surface policy gaps
  • Review local conventions

Know what context each stage needs

Each kind of context is fed in at the stage where it shapes a decision. Provide constraints before the decisions they govern, then retrieve detailed guidance when it becomes relevant. Excess irrelevant material can reduce effectiveness; critical policies may apply across several stages.

Context to add at each stage, where it is used and why it matters
StageContextWhere it is usedWhy it matters
1. Requirements and scopeBusiness domain intent, persona maps, scope boundariesThe PO/BA paths: SpecKit, the Socratic workflow and CLARAGrounds the user stories in the business problem, so the team does not build the wrong features.
2. Architecture and designShared architecture standards, integration recipes, decision templatesStory sequencing and investigation, before the technical requirements document (TRD) is writtenApplies structural constraints, such as authentication, logging and database schema, before work is sliced, so design flaws do not spread into every issue.
3. Compliance and governanceRegulatory and security policies, such as IM8 and ARCThe compliance audit of the TRDAudits the TRD against policy, so security controls are declared and resolved before coding.
4. ImplementationCoding practices, framework guides, API reference documentationThe build loop, through a knowledge-base queryGives the agent syntax, language features and library patterns, so code passes type checks, builds and tests.
5. Merge reviewRepository style, conventions and lint expectationsThe code review against the repository’s coding standardsKeeps changes consistent with the team’s style, naming rules and codebase conventions before merging.

Add business domain context

During requirements, the business domain enters through the specification files that the product owner (PO) or business analyst (BA) commits. How it is supplied depends on the PO/BA path:

  • Path 1, SpecKit: the PO or BA supplies domain context, terminology glossaries or functional requirements when generating the specification, so it uses the team’s vocabulary.
  • Path 2, Socratic workflow: the PO or BA points the agent at domain models, legacy codebase patterns or business-logic guides, so tickets and decision records stay in the team’s shared language.
  • Path 3, CLARA: the team places its domain documentation in the Confluence spaces or knowledge bases that CLARA queries, so personas, journey maps and specifications reflect the business.

Whichever path is used, the committed specification files carry the domain context into the developer harness as the source-of-truth handoff.

AIHow AI can help

AI can use supplied glossaries and business rules to draft stories in the team’s vocabulary. The PO or BA checks terms, scope and rules against the authoritative domain records and retains the corrected specification as the handoff.

Add shared standards and recipes

During planning, the harness matches each story to implementation standards. The base library is AppStandards, cloned from the shared repository or from a team fork.

AppStandards uses the Open Knowledge Format (OKF), which stores documentation as a version-controlled graph of Markdown concepts. Each folder has a catalogue of its contents, and each standard is split into focused files holding rules, code recipes and questions for challenging a design.

The harness maps every user story to the few standards it needs, such as multi-factor authentication or single sign-on, and later steps read only those files. Loading the whole catalogue can consume substantial context and introduce irrelevant material. Select the standards needed for the task and check that mandatory constraints remain available.

To add its own standards, a team structures them in the OKF layout, registers their location with the harness’s story-sequencing skill and tags its stories with the standard’s key. The standard then appears in the delivery plan for each tagged story.

AIHow AI can help

The agent can use the story’s selected standards and recipes to propose a technical approach. Engineers check that the references are current and applicable and that no mandatory constraint is missing; retain the selected standard keys and reviewed design with the story.

The local registration convention above tags stories. Current public Lesson 2 does not tag stories: it configures the standards catalogue, dependencies and concept-based node mapping in skills/project-horizon/configs/standards.md. Confirm the installed revision with the workflow owner before changing registration. Current course and revision limits.

Add coding practices to the knowledge base

During implementation, the agent retrieves coding practices and framework patterns from the organisation’s hosted Amazon Bedrock knowledge base. Inside the build loop, each file is routed to the relevant category of guidance; a React component file, for example, triggers a React query.

To add its own context, a team uploads its design guides, library documentation and coding conventions to the data source behind its knowledge base, runs a sync and points the harness at that knowledge base.

AIHow AI can help

Give the agent access to the relevant, synchronised library and framework guidance for the task. It can propose code using those patterns. Developers check API and version compatibility, run build and behaviour checks and retain the results with the change.

Add security and governance policies

Before work is sliced into issues, the compliance audit checks the TRD against the policy references held in the harness and writes a checklist report. Two references ship with the harness:

  • IM8: 36 application security checks in the documented Eitri policy pack, drawn from Instruction Manual 8; this is not a count of the entire policy framework.
  • ARC: 88 agentic AI governance checks in the documented Eitri policy pack, based on the Agentic Risk & Capability Framework. Confirm the pack version and applicable controls before an audit.

To include its own policies in the audit, a team writes its compliance checklist or internal security policy as a Markdown file and registers it with the harness. The audit assesses the document alongside IM8 and ARC. Enforce applicable controls through tests, access controls and pipeline checks; a written policy or model assessment alone does not enforce them.

AIHow AI can help

The compliance skill can compare the TRD with the registered policy references and write findings. Reviewers check the applicable policy version and reproduce the claimed gap or control evidence. Keep the checklist report and resolved findings; enforce controls through the documented technical checks.

The public Eitri lessons describe an 88-check ARC policy pack, while the current ARC framework site lists 86 controls across 46 risks. These counts describe different artefacts; confirm the pack revision and control mapping with its owner rather than replacing 88 with 86. Training scope.

Add review rules

At the end of the development loop, changes are checked against the repository’s own conventions: formatting rules, naming, design principles and lint-like expectations. A team keeps them in one coding standards file at the root of the application repository.

The code review checks each change against this file, both inside the build loop and at closeout. Where the file is silent, the review falls back to a baseline of common code smells.

AIHow AI can help

AI can compare a diff with the repository’s coding standards and flag apparent inconsistencies. The developer checks each finding against the actual rule and changed behaviour, makes justified corrections and retains the review and check results.

Set up your team’s context

A new project team can use this checklist to prepare its context. Confirm each source’s revision and access, test that the installed skill retrieves the intended files, and verify that mandatory policies remain available at the relevant decision points.

  1. Write local coding rules. Record naming, architecture patterns and formatting expectations in the repository’s coding standards file.
  2. Configure the knowledge base. Upload coding standards, library documentation and technical guidelines to the team’s knowledge base, and point the harness at it.
  3. Connect architecture standards. Structure the team’s standards in the OKF layout and confirm the registration convention for the installed revision; the local story-tag approach differs from current public Lesson 2’s node mapping.
  4. Define security policies. Write any additional corporate security policies as Markdown and register them with the harness.
  5. Declare architecture boundary tests. Let the harness scan the project and propose boundary rules, review and customise them, then generate the tests.

Next step: complete items 1 and 5 first, because they need only the repository. Then take a first story through planning and note which context the agent asked for but could not find.

Eitri status and version: verify installed revisions and enforced controls.

  7. GovTech. Agentic Risk & Capability Framework (ARC). Governance framework underlying the documented TRD audit.
